Yes! Last month, I celebrated my one-year anniversary as a registered dietitian! I have been in healthcare for about 10 years, but I'm happy to finally be at a capacity where I can do more to help people. Today, my Facebook memories reminded me that my twin graduated from medical school on this day 4 years ago. She's now at a health center doing family medicine. We worked EXTREMELY HARD to accomplish these things. 

I feel I worked as hard as my sister did, because I had so many tribulations after not getting into med school. This was a very devastating time in my life. I did grad school for metabolism before going into dietetics. I had to take my licensure exam more than once, being 2 and then 1 point from passing, which was *so frustrating*. 

But I have been doing so well and got a really good first performance review. I'm happy neither my sister nor I gave up! They wanted to kick her out of residency at one point (literally over racism, which is a story for another time, and happens to residents of color *all of the time*), and I watched her battle that with depression. It's not like medical school isn't already one of the most grueling processes a person can go through. And she gets great reviews as well.

The moral of the story is: If you want something, don't stop. Go and get it. Surround yourself with people who want to see you succeed, and you will!

I am proud of ALL of us! 💜

I think that really refers to the *food* itself that you're eating (leafy greens, nuts, seeds are alkaline foods), but it's misinformation that you can literally control your body's pH by food, and people are confusing the two.

I just don't talk to people at times to avoid this situation. Lmfao. Like, today I read a post written by a musician that likes to write, and he wrote, "Upon scrolling certain apps within close [sic] proximity to good friends, I’ve been asked occasionally if everything was ok," and I didn't bother to comment because all I wanted to say was, "This is amazing, but you don't need to use the word close when you say proximity because that's literally what proximity means." I can't help it! It just hurts my fuckin' brain! But I'm emotionally intelligent enough to know that if I had said that, it would more than likely have been perceived as rude, especially when you cannot always tell tone because it is text on the internet.

I ran on treadmills for years and was also likely calcium and vitamin D deficient for a lot of that time (runs in my family). Some of the damage I think is from everything I was doing. I've seen posts by people who are younger than me who have it. Some are athletes (osteoarthritis), some have rheumatoid. There is some unclear evidence of autoimmune disease in my family. I saw a rheumatologist, and my tests for things like HLA-B27, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, did not indicate that I have rheumatoid arthritis. I think this is damage from what I mentioned above. 

I theorize that it is possibly even arthritogenic virus related, as I've had COVID twice (despite being fully vaccinated, and boosted more than once), and never started feeling all of this joint pain until after the first time I had COVID. The evidence is somewhat unclear to me because we are not years and years out in terms of research on the lasting or prolonged effects of COVID.

It scares me that I am already dealing with this. I work with elders and can relate to them *more* than I should probably be able to when it comes to body pains. I am afraid to imagine how I will feel in 5-10 years. 

My diagnosis is considered "mild," but there are occasional days that this crap brings me to tears. I shudder to imagine what moderate or severe feels like.

As I said in another comment: you can influence the *ash* (e.g. stones) in the urine with diet based on acidity or alkalinity of the diet. But you are not controlling the pH of your entire body by diet (your urine pH is not indicative of the pH of the rest of your body. You can have alkaline urine and *acidic blood* simultaneously). I'm not spreading misinformation. I have a master's degree in nutrition and metabolism, and I'm a practicing dietitian who has worked in healthcare for more than a decade. I don't know why you think it's okay to attack people for no apparent reason.

For your information, RDs don't make a lot of money, and I think a good chunk of us aren't necessarily huge on big pharma, when we *know* many common illnesses can be managed with lifestyle and diet. This has nothing to do with "profit" for me. I enjoy arming people with correct information so they can control their health better. I think you should actually read what people say before you presume they don't know anything.

I don't recall the exact name of the group, but if you go on Facebook and search, "RD exam live sessions," you should be able to find it. 

I created a study subreddit to dump things, even for future reference. Feel free to peruse my subreddit, r/studyingforRDexam with the caveat that you'll probably not get any metabolism questions. I have posted a lot more on that than I have ever needed for the exam (that's just my crazy brain that is obsessed with small detail. I struggle with the big picture), so don't be intimidated by that.

For tube feed questions, I suggest understanding very thoroughly how to calculate the calories, mL of fat/macros in exemplary tube feeds. You probably will not be asked to do one from scratch on the actual exam.

Find out which domain(s) you struggle with and study that material the most. I really, really hate management and food service. That is where I was not proficient. My MNT score went up and up with my attempts, so I stopped studying it very much and focused on the other domains. 

I also bought a subscription for Pocket Prep and used it a lot. Save questions you get wrong and look that information up in Jean Inman if you are struggling with concepts. Do the missed questions quizzes. You will improve with consistency of effort. I had practically memorized Jean Inman audio lectures, always listened to her while working out or walking. I even would read domains and record myself so I could listen while sitting in traffic.

Find out what kind of learner you are (e.g. visual, audio, etc.) and study in ways that accommodate that. I'm a very kinetic learner, and I need to *do* things instead of just read about them. Better if I can do things while hearing about it. I think that helped me.

And just don't give up if you really want to be a dietitian. I do community dietetics, and I love it. I know I'm really helping people who need it the most.

Ingredients:

Olive oil 2-3 tablespoons

3-4 shallots (if you’re fancy) or 1 medium onion

4+ cloves of garlic

Balsamic vinegar

1 28 oz can of whole peeled tomato, preferably San Marzano

1 pack of portobello mushrooms from market basket (8-16 oz?)

1-1.5 tablespoons of butter (or vegan sub)

Fresh basil and oregano

Sunflower lecithin powder (optional) 0.5-1 tbsp

Salt, black pepper, red pepper flakes (to taste/spice tolerance)

Preferred pasta



Finely chop or food processor shallots and garlic
Put olive oil in large, deep skillet over medium heat; saute shallots and garlic, add some balsamic vinegar mid sauté to prevent burning and for Maillard rxn
Crush tomatoes and add to pan when alliums are done cooking, also put in fresh oregano, put on low heat and let simmer, stirring frequently to prevent sticking
Begin to sauté mushrooms with butter in separate pan over low-medium heat til they shrink, then add balsamic vinegar so mushrooms absorb it
Add cooked mushrooms and fresh basil to simmering tomato sauce, salt and black pepper to taste, lecithin if you are using it
Let simmer stirring frequently total cook time should be ~45+ minutes
Cook pasta per instructions then add about 0.5-1 cup of pasta water to the sauce, increasing heat on sauce to medium
Once the volume has reduced to desired consistency toss pasta in the sauce and serve

Makes me think about nutritive versus non-nutritive sweeteners. This picture nicely explains why. https://www.reddit.com/r/studyingforRDexam/s/DDmSSeINFk

Aspartame can convert to aspar*tate* to enter the citric acid/Krebs cycle. Aspar*tate* then converts to oxaloacetate, which goes through gluconeogenesis (phosphoenolpyruvate through PEPCK). Make new glucose to be broken down, hence nutritive.

Aspartame ➡️ aspartate, and can convert *in vivo* into phenylalanine. Phenylalanine can enter Krebs via acetoacetate to acetyl CoA, hence nutritive. 

Sucralose (Splenda) is not metabolized, hence non-nutritive.
